--- title: "Using BlackMarble Nighttime Lights Data in R - Interactive Tutorial" output: learnr::tutorial: progressive: true allow_skip: true runtime: shiny_prerendered description: "Interactive tutorial providing an introduction to spatial analysis in R and for working with BlackMarble nighttime lights data." --- # Introduction to Spatial Analysis and BlackMarble Data Welcome to this interactive tutorial on using BlackMarble nighttime lights data in R! This tutorial will guide you through: - Fundamentals of spatial data analysis in R - Working with vector and raster data - Using the BlackMarble dataset for economic analysis - Creating visualizations and maps ## Learning Objectives By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to: 1. Load and manipulate spatial data in R 2. Work with BlackMarble nighttime lights data 3. Perform spatial operations and analysis 4. Create static and interactive maps 5. Extract meaningful insights from geospatial data --- # Setup and Required Packages Before we begin, let's ensure you have all the necessary packages installed. The following packages are essential for spatial analysis in R: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Core spatial packages library(sf) # Simple Features for vector data library(terra) # Spatial data analysis library(leaflet) # Interactive maps # Data manipulation library(dplyr) # Data manipulation library(ggplot2) # Plotting # BlackMarble specific library(blackmarbler) # Access BlackMarble data # Check if packages loaded successfully sessionInfo() ```
::: ## Spatial Analysis Packages Overview This section summarizes some of the most commonly used packages for spatial analysis. * [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/): Package for working with vector data. (sf = simple features) * [terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/): Package for working with both raster data and vector data. * [tidyterra](https://dieghernan.github.io/tidyterra/): Provides methods common to tidyverse for working with terra objects; also provides additional geoms for plotting spatial data using `ggplot` * [leaflet](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/) R interface to leaflet, a JavaScript library for interactive maps ### Exercise: Package Check Try loading the main spatial packages: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Load the main spatial packages library(sf) library(terra) library(dplyr) # Check if they loaded successfully cat("Packages loaded successfully!") ```
::: --- # Working with Vector Data Vector data represents discrete features with clear boundaries, such as administrative boundaries, roads, or points of interest. ## Loading Vector Data Let's start by loading some administrative boundary data for Nigeria: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Load Nigeria administrative boundaries from existing data nga_adm1_sf <- read_sf("/Users/ssarva/ntl-training-1/data/gadm/nga_adm1.geojson") # Examine the data structure class(nga_adm1_sf) head(nga_adm1_sf) ```
::: ### Exercise: Explore Vector Data Explore the Nigeria administrative data: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Check the dimensions of the data dim(nga_adm1_sf) # Look at column names names(nga_adm1_sf) # Check the coordinate reference system st_crs(nga_adm1_sf) ```
::: ## Basic Vector Operations ### Plotting Vector Data ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Simple plot plot(nga_adm1_sf["NAME_1"]) # Using ggplot2 ggplot(nga_adm1_sf) + geom_sf() + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Nigeria Administrative Level 1 Boundaries") ```
::: ### Exercise: Create Your Own Plot Try creating a plot with different aesthetics: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Create a custom plot of Nigeria boundaries # Hint: Try adding fill colors, different themes, or labels ```
::: ::: {.cell}
```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nga_adm1_sf) + geom_sf(fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue", size = 0.5) + theme_void() + labs(title = "Nigeria Administrative Boundaries", subtitle = "Level 1 Administrative Units") + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) ```
::: --- # Interactive Maps with Leaflet Leaflet provides an excellent way to create interactive maps. Let's create some interactive visualizations: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Basic leaflet map leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% # Add default OpenStreetMap tiles addPolygons(data = nga_adm1_sf, fillOpacity = 0.3, weight = 2, popup = ~NAME_1) ```
::: ### Exercise: Enhanced Leaflet Map Try enhancing the leaflet map with different features: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Create an enhanced leaflet map # Try adding: # - Different color schemes # - Labels # - Custom popups # - Different basemaps ```
::: ::: {.cell}
```{.r .cell-code} leaflet(nga_adm1_sf) %>% addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>% addPolygons( fillColor = "blue", fillOpacity = 0.4, color = "darkblue", weight = 2, popup = ~paste("State:", NAME_1, "
", "Type:", ENGTYPE_1), label = ~NAME_1, highlightOptions = highlightOptions( weight = 3, fillOpacity = 0.7, bringToFront = TRUE ) ) ```
::: --- # Introduction to BlackMarble Data BlackMarble is a NASA Earth science data product that provides global nighttime lights data from the VIIRS Day/Night Band (DNB) sensor. This data is valuable for: - Economic activity monitoring - Population density estimation - Urbanization studies - Disaster impact assessment - Energy consumption analysis ## Key Features of BlackMarble Data 1. **High Resolution**: 500m spatial resolution 2. **Global Coverage**: Worldwide data availability 3. **Regular Updates**: Monthly composites 4. **Quality Control**: Filtered for clouds, stray light, and other artifacts ### Exercise: Understanding NTL Applications Think about and discuss potential applications of nighttime lights data in your field of work: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # What could you use nighttime lights data for? # Consider economic, social, or environmental applications # Type your thoughts as comments: # Economic applications: # # Social applications: # # Environmental applications: # ```
::: --- # Working with BlackMarble Data in R The `blackmarbler` package provides convenient access to BlackMarble data through Google Earth Engine. ## Setting Up BlackMarble Access ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Note: This requires Google Earth Engine authentication # For this tutorial, we'll use pre-downloaded data # To set up your own access: # library(blackmarbler) # # # Set your Google Earth Engine credentials # # Follow instructions at: https://worldbank.github.io/blackmarbler/ ```
::: ## Loading Sample BlackMarble Data Let's work with some sample BlackMarble data: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # In a real workflow, you would use: # ntl_raster <- bm_raster( # roi = nga_adm1_sf, # product_id = "VNP46A4", # date = "2023-01-01", # bearer = bearer_token # ) # For this tutorial, let's simulate some NTL data set.seed(123) ntl_values <- runif(nrow(nga_adm1_sf), min = 0.1, max = 5.0) nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean <- ntl_values # View the data head(nga_adm1_sf[c("NAME_1", "ntl_mean")]) ```
::: ### Exercise: Explore NTL Data Explore the nighttime lights data we just added: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate basic statistics for the NTL data summary(nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean) # Find the state with highest and lowest NTL max_ntl <- nga_adm1_sf[which.max(nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean), "NAME_1"] min_ntl <- nga_adm1_sf[which.min(nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean), "NAME_1"] print(paste("Highest NTL:", max_ntl$NAME_1)) print(paste("Lowest NTL:", min_ntl$NAME_1)) ```
::: --- # Visualizing BlackMarble Data ## Static Maps with ggplot2 ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Create a choropleth map of nighttime lights ggplot(nga_adm1_sf) + geom_sf(aes(fill = ntl_mean)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "NTL\nMean") + theme_void() + labs(title = "Average Nighttime Lights by State in Nigeria", subtitle = "Simulated data for demonstration") ```
::: ### Exercise: Customize the Static Map Try customizing the map with different color schemes and themes: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Customize the NTL map # Try different: # - Color palettes (scale_fill_*) # - Themes # - Labels and titles ```
::: ::: {.cell}
```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nga_adm1_sf) + geom_sf(aes(fill = ntl_mean), color = "white", size = 0.3) + scale_fill_gradient2( low = "navy", mid = "yellow", high = "red", midpoint = median(nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean), name = "Nighttime\nLights" ) + theme_void() + theme( plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12), legend.position = "bottom" ) + labs( title = "Nighttime Lights Intensity", subtitle = "Nigeria Administrative Level 1", caption = "Data: Simulated for demonstration purposes" ) ```
::: ## Interactive Maps with NTL Data ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Create an interactive map with NTL data # Define color palette pal <- colorNumeric(palette = "viridis", domain = nga_adm1_sf$ntl_mean) leaflet(nga_adm1_sf) %>% addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.DarkMatter) %>% addPolygons( fillColor = ~pal(ntl_mean), fillOpacity = 0.7, color = "white", weight = 1, popup = ~paste("State:", NAME_1, "
", "NTL Mean:", round(ntl_mean, 3)), label = ~paste(NAME_1, ":", round(ntl_mean, 3)) ) %>% addLegend( position = "bottomright", pal = pal, values = ~ntl_mean, title = "NTL Mean" ) ```
::: ### Exercise: Interactive Map Enhancement Enhance the interactive map with additional features: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Enhance the interactive map # Try adding: # - Different basemaps # - Highlight effects # - Additional popup information # - Custom icons or markers ```
::: --- # Spatial Analysis with NTL Data ## Basic Statistical Analysis ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Basic descriptive statistics nga_adm1_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% # Remove geometry for easier analysis select(NAME_1, ntl_mean) %>% arrange(desc(ntl_mean)) %>% head(10) # Create a histogram ggplot(nga_adm1_sf, aes(x = ntl_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Distribution of Nighttime Lights", x = "NTL Mean Value", y = "Count of States") ```
::: ### Exercise: Correlation Analysis Let's explore relationships between NTL and other variables: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Add some simulated variables for analysis nga_adm1_sf$population <- runif(nrow(nga_adm1_sf), 1000000, 10000000) nga_adm1_sf$urban_pct <- runif(nrow(nga_adm1_sf), 10, 80) # Calculate correlations cor_data <- nga_adm1_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(ntl_mean, population, urban_pct) cor(cor_data) # Create a scatter plot ggplot(nga_adm1_sf, aes(x = urban_pct, y = ntl_mean)) + geom_point(aes(size = population), alpha = 0.6) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Relationship between Urban Percentage and Nighttime Lights", x = "Urban Percentage", y = "NTL Mean", size = "Population") ```
::: --- # Advanced Applications ## Time Series Analysis Concept While we're working with simulated data, in practice you would analyze temporal trends: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Conceptual example of time series analysis # In practice, you would load multiple months/years of data months <- month.name nga_lagos <- nga_adm1_sf[nga_adm1_sf$NAME_1 == "Lagos", ] # Simulate monthly data for Lagos set.seed(456) monthly_ntl <- data.frame( month = factor(months, levels = months), ntl_value = 2.5 + 0.3 * sin(1:12) + rnorm(12, 0, 0.1) ) # Plot time series ggplot(monthly_ntl, aes(x = month, y = ntl_value, group = 1)) + geom_line(color = "blue", size = 1) + geom_point(color = "red", size = 2) + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) + labs(title = "Simulated Monthly NTL Trends - Lagos State", x = "Month", y = "NTL Value") ```
::: ### Exercise: Seasonal Analysis Analyze the seasonal patterns in the simulated data: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Analyze seasonal patterns # Calculate quarterly averages monthly_ntl$quarter <- rep(paste("Q", 1:4), each = 3)[1:12] quarterly_summary <- monthly_ntl %>% group_by(quarter) %>% summarise( mean_ntl = mean(ntl_value), sd_ntl = sd(ntl_value), .groups = 'drop' ) print(quarterly_summary) # Create a quarterly comparison plot ggplot(quarterly_summary, aes(x = quarter, y = mean_ntl)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_ntl - sd_ntl, ymax = mean_ntl + sd_ntl), width = 0.2) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Quarterly NTL Averages", x = "Quarter", y = "Mean NTL Value") ```
::: --- # Summary and Next Steps Congratulations! You've completed the interactive BlackMarble tutorial. You've learned: 1. ✅ How to work with spatial data in R 2. ✅ Basic operations with vector data 3. ✅ Creating static and interactive maps 4. ✅ Understanding BlackMarble nighttime lights data 5. ✅ Performing spatial analysis and visualization ## Key Takeaways - **sf** and **terra** are essential packages for spatial analysis in R - **leaflet** provides excellent interactive mapping capabilities - BlackMarble data offers valuable insights into human activity patterns - Combining spatial data with statistical analysis reveals important relationships ## Further Learning - Explore the [blackmarbler package documentation](https://worldbank.github.io/blackmarbler/) - Learn more about [spatial analysis in R](https://r-spatial.org/) - Practice with real BlackMarble data from your region of interest - Investigate advanced applications like change detection and predictive modeling ### Final Exercise: Project Planning Think about a research question you could address using nighttime lights data: ::: {.cell exercise='true'}
```{.r .cell-code} # Plan your own BlackMarble project # Consider: # 1. Research question: # # 2. Geographic area of interest: # # 3. Time period for analysis: # # 4. Additional data sources needed: # # 5. Expected outcomes: # ```
